strengths: The paper is simple and easy to follow and understand. It gently introduces the problem and smoothly translates to the proposed method.
The proposed algorithm (SODA) is simple and neat.
The provided experimental results shows the effectiveness of the proposed SODA compared to other baselines under the streaming evaluation.

This paper contributes with both theoretical and empirical insights.
Problem setting: The problem of Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) detection with stream data is a relevant and interesting topic for the reliable machine learning community.
Presentation: The paper is well-structured and clearly written in most parts.
Experiments: Extensive experiments have been conducted in this paper to validate the proposed methods.
This paper is well organized and easy to follow.
The proposed algorithm is simple and easy to implement with many OOD loss and shows empirical success on several benchmark datasets.
weaknesses: Missing definition of performance measures such as FPR and AUROC.
Missing rationale behind choosing the datasets in Table 1, e.g., why SCHN considered OOD compared to CIFAR and how to quantify the distance between evaluated distribution and training one.
The experiments consider stationary datasets such as ImageNet and CIFAR-10 where the stream is synthetically constructed; realistic benchmarks with time-defined streams should be used.

Discussion of limitation: SODA may fail on streams with very small visual variations, potentially overfitting the network parameters and failing to generalize on new batches; a limitation discussion should be included.
The solution seems less technical to me. This needs further discussion during rebuttal.
The current version seems to embed an OOD detector into a naive online learning framework.
This paper claims its novelty in online OOD detection, but [1] is also designed for online OOD detection; a comparison and clarification of the improvement over [1] is required.
Could you specify which items in (2) and (3) are designed specially for an online non-stantioanry environment?
In the current SODA, OOD detector and classifier are updated at every new t, which may not always be beneficial; the necessity of updating at every t should be explained.
Will SODA have a high computational cost? Please also specify the computational cost for the update process.

Originality and Significance: The proposed method appears to be a direct application of classical Online Gradient Descent (OGD) with cross-entropy loss, and the regret analysis is standard; the claim of handling non‑stationary OOD data is not convincingly differentiated from existing online convex optimization frameworks.

Feedback assumption: The algorithm assumes labels of OOD data are available after prediction, which is a strong assumption that undermines the OOD detection challenge; the difference from supervised online learning and guarantees for the unsupervised loss are unclear.

Theoretical analysis: The statement of Theorem 3.1 is informal, lacking conditions on loss functions and parameters; the analysis relies on convexity and a linear model, while the main paper uses a neural network, creating a discrepancy that should be addressed.

The proposed algorithm requires strong supervision feedback on whether each instance is OOD during online learning, which is difficult to satisfy in real‑world applications and oversimplifies the learning task.
The unsupervised version lacks solid theoretical guarantees, limiting the applicability of the method.

The theoretical results are well‑established in online learning literature and thus limit the technical contribution; they are straightforward when a specific convex loss is specified, and the work uses static regret instead of adaptive or dynamic regret for non‑stationarity.

Determining the hyperparameter λ for OOD detection before and during online learning is challenging; the paper does not explain how λ is set in experiments or how it affects performance, and no code is published.
